Combined deletion of Cabp1 and Cabp2 produces much greater calcium-channel inactivation and sustained-release impairment than Cabp2 deletion alone. At depolarized holding potentials, sustained exocytosis can be abolished. Recovery after prolonged sinusoidal stimulation is delayed, whereas recovery after a shorter strong depolarization behaves differently. Ribbon-synapse abundance is retained at the examined early age, but BK-channel clusters are smaller. Neonatal Cabp2 delivery partially rescues channel function, synaptic release and hearing.

Reduced availability of presynaptic CaV1.3 channels is proposed to decrease effective transmitter delivery to auditory afferents. Whole-cell capacitance assays did not show reduced exocytosis in Cabp2-only knockout hair cells; some sustained responses were increased, possibly through extrasynaptic release. In contrast, combined Cabp1/Cabp2 deletion directly reduces sustained exocytosis, especially at depolarized holding potentials. The double-knockout result supports the mechanism but cannot be assigned unchanged to human DFNB93.
